# CNNs: Making the Filters Learnable {#sec-08-cnn}

@sec-07-filters-convolution applied a fixed local kernel with shared coefficients at
every position. We now keep that spatial structure and optimize the coefficients against a
task loss.

To do so, we declare the kernel coefficients to be learnable parameters. That single change is
the core of this chapter. Everything else introduced here (channels, padding, stride and
pooling) turns the learnable filter into a working network. By the end of the chapter we will
have assembled [LeNet](https://doi.org/10.1109/5.726791), trained it on the Fashion-MNIST
images of @sec-06-generalization-inductive-bias, and repeated that chapter's shift experiment
to test whether LeNet tolerates the shift better than the MLP did.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Load imports and the Fashion-MNIST subset.
:::

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| code-summary: "Code: imports and the Fashion-MNIST subset"
#| code-fold: false
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
development = torch.load("../../data/fashion-train.pt")
holdout = torch.load("../../data/fashion-test.pt")
X_dev = development["X"].float().unsqueeze(1) / 255.0  # (1200, 1, 28, 28)
y_dev, classes = development["y"], development["classes"]
X_test = holdout["X"].float().unsqueeze(1) / 255.0     # (600, 1, 28, 28)
y_test = holdout["y"]

split = torch.randperm(len(X_dev), generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(6050))
fit_idx, val_idx = split[:1000], split[1000:]
X_tr, y_tr = X_dev[fit_idx], y_dev[fit_idx]      # (1000,1,28,28), (1000,)
X_val, y_val = X_dev[val_idx], y_dev[val_idx]    # (200,1,28,28), (200,)
```
::::
Note the shapes. In Part I our MLPs flattened every image into a vector of 784 pixels,
discarding its two-dimensional arrangement at the first layer. A convolutional network keeps
that geometry: the images stay rectangular grids, and they gain an explicit *channel*
dimension, whose purpose we explain below.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The book's batch convention: NCHW

Throughout this book, every image **batch** uses PyTorch's **NCHW** order: (batch,
channels, height, width). A single grayscale batch is therefore shaped `(1, 1, 28,
28)`. `Conv2d` can also accept an unbatched `(C, H, W)` input, but keeping the batch
dimension explicit makes downstream shapes predictable. The kernels of a conv layer
are stored in a 4-D tensor too: (out-channels,
in-channels, height, width). This bookkeeping is a common source of
errors in convolutional code: when a shape error appears, count dimensions before
changing anything else. @sec-07-filters-convolution's `conv2d` helper hid this with `x[None, None]`;
from here on we handle it in the open.
:::

## Learning a kernel from input–output pairs {#nine-numbers-learned}

Consider a game. A feature detector, one of the fixed filters of @sec-07-filters-convolution,
is hidden from us; we observe only what it does: images go in, feature maps come out.
Our job is to build a detector that matches it.

The tools of Part I suffice. A kernel applied by @eq-crosscorr is
just nine numbers entering a dot product $\rightarrow$ the output is differentiable
with respect to those numbers $\rightarrow$ gradient descent applies. Start from a
random kernel and run the loop we have run since @sec-01-linear-regression: predict $\rightarrow$
measure $\rightarrow$ step.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Compute the hidden `mystery` kernel's `target` maps on 256 garments and draw a small
   random `K`.
2. Recover a mystery kernel by gradient descent.
:::

```{python}
#| label: learn-kernel
#| code-summary: "Code: recover a mystery kernel by gradient descent"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
mystery = torch.tensor([[-1., 0., 1.],
                        [-2., 0., 2.],
                        [-1., 0., 1.]])            # (don't peek)
imgs = X_tr[:256]                                  # (256, 1, 28, 28)
with torch.no_grad():
    target = F.conv2d(imgs, mystery[None, None])   # what the detector does

torch.manual_seed(0)
K = 0.1 * torch.randn(1, 1, 3, 3)
K_init = K.clone().squeeze()
K.requires_grad_(True)

lr = 0.5
# [2]
for step in range(601):
    pred = F.conv2d(imgs, K)                       # predict
    loss = F.mse_loss(pred, target)                # measure
    loss.backward()
    with torch.no_grad():                          # step
        K -= lr * K.grad
        K.grad.zero_()
    if step % 200 == 0:
        print(f"step {step:3d}   loss {loss.item():.2e}")

print(f"\nlearned kernel, rounded:\n{K.detach().squeeze().round(decimals=2)}")
print(f"max |learned - mystery| = {(K.detach().squeeze() - mystery).abs().max():.3f}")
```
::::
The loss falls more than five orders of magnitude, and the learned kernel is the vertical Sobel
detector to within 0.02 in every entry. Gradient descent, given nothing but
input–output pairs, has *recovered* a filter that computer-vision researchers
originally designed by hand.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-learned-kernel
#| fig-alt: "Three three-by-three heatmaps compare a disordered random kernel, a learned signed pattern, and the vertical Sobel pattern. The learned and Sobel panels have nearly identical positive and negative columns."
#| fig-cap: "The mystery-detector game. Left: the random starting kernel. Middle: the kernel gradient descent found from input–output pairs alone. Right: the hand-crafted vertical Sobel detector from @sec-07-filters-convolution. The middle kernel was fitted without any definition of an edge."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7, 2.6))
lim = 2.2
for ax, k, title in zip(axes, [K_init, K.detach().squeeze(), mystery],
                        ["random start", "learned", "Sobel (truth)"]):
    im = ax.imshow(k, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-lim, vmax=lim)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.8)
plt.show()
```
::: {.callout-tip}
## Kernels learned from data

Deep learning for vision is that experiment at scale. @sec-07-filters-convolution ended with the bottleneck: someone has to design the kernel,
choosing its coefficients for a specific low-level operation such as smoothing or
detecting intensity changes. *What if
the template were learnable?* A convolutional network makes it learnable:
it puts the coefficients on the gradient tape and fits them to the task loss, with
machinery we have used since @sec-04-training-loss-sgd.
:::

Two differences make the real thing *harder* than the game, not easier. First, the game was rigged: the target came from a known kernel,
so a perfect answer existed and the loss surface was a clean convex bowl (the output
is linear in the kernel $K$, and squared error in a linear map is @sec-01-linear-regression's setting all over
again). Second, and more important: **in a real CNN, nobody supplies the target
feature maps.** The only supervision is the classification loss at the far end of the
network. The gradient flows backward through every layer (exactly the mechanics of
@sec-05-backpropagation) and the kernels that emerge are whatever detectors the task
loss favors. We chose Sobel here; a trained network may arrive at kernels that match
no named filter.

Backpropagation through a convolutional layer applies the accumulation rule of @sec-05-backpropagation:
a quantity used in several places of a computation receives the sum of the gradients from all
of them. The kernel is such a quantity. In the notation of @eq-crosscorr, write the kernel as
$V$ (the $K$ of the game) and the output map as $H$. The weight $[V]_{u,v}$ enters every
output entry $[H]_{i,j}$, each time multiplied by the pixel $[X]_{i+u,\,j+v}$, so

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial [V]_{u,v}} \;=\; \sum_{i,j} \delta_{i,j}\,[X]_{i+u,\,j+v},
\qquad \delta_{i,j} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial [H]_{i,j}},
$$

with one more sum over the images of the batch. The gradient is itself a cross-correlation with
the roles exchanged: the map of sensitivities $\delta$ acts as the kernel and slides over
$X$, and its $k \times k$ stops give the entries of $\partial L/\partial V$. With the default
`reduction="mean"` of `F.mse_loss`, each $\delta_{i,j}$ carries a factor of one over the
number of averaged entries. Weight sharing on the forward pass therefore means summed gradients
on the backward pass: every patch of every image contributes to the update of the one shared
template.

## Channels: from one detector to many {#from-one-detector-to-a-layer-of-detectives}

One learnable kernel gives one feature map, and one feature map records one pattern: a
vertical edge, a horizontal edge, a local average. The examples of fixed filters in @sec-07-filters-convolution
showed that an image carries many such patterns at once, and a classifier needs evidence about
several of them at every position. A layer therefore applies several kernels to the same input,
a team of specialized detectors, each producing its own feature map. Their responses at one
position form a vector, and the representation gains a dimension: the **channels**.

Channels enter a convolutional layer at two places, with different roles:

- **Out-channels add kernels.** A conv layer with 6 output channels owns 6
  independent kernels and produces a stack of 6 feature maps.
- **In-channels let each kernel span the whole stack.** The next layer's input is that
  6-deep stack, so the input at each position is a vector of 6 responses rather than one
  pixel. Each kernel of the next layer therefore grows a third dimension: a $6 \times 5
  \times 5$ volume that covers all six incoming maps at once.

For an input stack $X$ with $C_{\text{in}}$ channels, output feature map
$o \in \{1, \dots, C_{\text{out}}\}$ is

$$
[H_o]_{i,j} \;=\; b_o \;+\; \sum_{c=1}^{C_{\text{in}}}\;
\Bigl(\,\sum_{u=-\Delta}^{\Delta}\;\sum_{v=-\Delta}^{\Delta}
[V_{o,c}]_{u,v}\,[X_c]_{i+u,\,j+v}\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-conv-layer}

and a pointwise activation follows; as in @sec-07-filters-convolution, the kernel is
$k \times k$ with $k = 2\Delta + 1$. The inner double sum is the cross-correlation of @eq-crosscorr,
applied to input channel $c$ with the slice $V_{o,c}$ of the kernel; the outer sum adds the
$C_{\text{in}}$ results, and $b_o$ is the bias of output channel $o$. The
computation for one output pixel is one dot product between a
$C_{\text{in}} \times k \times k$ patch of the input and the $C_{\text{in}} \times k \times k$
kernel of output channel $o$, plus the bias $b_o$. A dense layer of an MLP takes a dot product
across all of its input features; a convolutional layer takes the same kind of dot product
across all input channels but only a small spatial window, and slides it over the grid. The
recipe of the layer (dot products, bias, activation) is the MLP's; only the wiring of the
linear part differs.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Build `conv1` (1 to 6 channels) and `conv2` (6 to 16), then feed one garment through
   both with ReLU.
2. Run one grayscale image through two conv layers.
:::

```{python}
#| label: channels
#| code-summary: "Code: one grayscale image through two conv layers"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=6, kernel_size=5, padding=2)
conv2 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=6, out_channels=16, kernel_size=5)

x = X_tr[:1]                                   # (1, 1, 28, 28): one garment
h1 = F.relu(conv1(x))
h2 = F.relu(conv2(h1))
# [2]
print(f"input   {tuple(x.shape)}")
print(f"conv1   {tuple(h1.shape)}   kernels: {tuple(conv1.weight.shape)}")
print(f"conv2   {tuple(h2.shape)}  kernels: {tuple(conv2.weight.shape)}")
```
::::
Each kernel of `conv2` spans all six maps of `conv1`, so it computes combinations of the first
layer's responses rather than of raw pixels. If earlier channels respond to edges of different
orientations, a later channel can combine them into a response to corners or crossings. We
build one such combination by hand on a filled square: two first-layer channels compute
vertical and horizontal edge energy, and one second-layer kernel with equal positive weights on
both channels sums them over a local window (@fig-corner-detector).

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Make a filled-square image and compute edge magnitudes `v` and `h` with `sobel_v` and
   its transpose.
2. Run a corner detector built from two edge experts.
:::

```{python}
#| label: corner-detector-values
#| code-summary: "Code: a corner detector built from two edge detectors"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
square = torch.zeros(28, 28)
square[7:21, 7:21] = 1.0
sobel_v = torch.tensor([[-1., 0., 1.], [-2., 0., 2.], [-1., 0., 1.]])
v = F.conv2d(square[None, None], sobel_v[None, None], padding=1).abs()
h = F.conv2d(square[None, None], sobel_v.T.contiguous()[None, None], padding=1).abs()

# [2]
experts = torch.cat([v, h], dim=1)              # (1, 2, 28, 28): two reports
corner_k = torch.full((1, 2, 5, 5), 1 / 50)     # one kernel, spanning both
corners = F.conv2d(experts, corner_k, padding=2).squeeze()
```
::::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-corner-detector
#| fig-alt: "Four grayscale panels progress from a filled square to vertical-edge energy, horizontal-edge energy, and their combined response. Only the last panel concentrates its brightest responses at all four corners."
#| fig-cap: "Combining two edge maps by hand. The input is a 28×28 image of zeros whose central 14×14 block (rows and columns 7 to 20) is set to 1. Two first-layer channels compute edge energy, the absolute response to the vertical Sobel kernel and to its transpose, each with padding 1. One second-layer kernel of shape 2×5×5, every entry 1/50 (@eq-conv-layer with two input channels, padding 2), sums both edge maps over a local window, and its response is strongest near the square's four corners."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(9, 2.5))
panels = [(square, "input"), (v.squeeze(), "vertical-edge expert"),
          (h.squeeze(), "horizontal-edge expert"), (corners, "their reader: corners")]
for ax, (t, title) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.imshow(t, cmap="gray"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
For this square, the combined response is strongest near the corners, where both channels
respond. The kernel only sums local edge responses, so a sufficiently strong response in
either channel could also produce a large output. In a trained CNN, the coefficients of these
combinations are learned from the task loss.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Modules and functional operations

`nn.Conv2d` stores its kernels and biases as registered
parameters. `F.conv2d` applies the operation using tensors
supplied as arguments. Both support differentiation: the first
experiment optimizes the kernel $K$ directly, while LeNet uses modules
to organize its trainable parameters.
:::

## Padding and stride: controlling the output size {#padding-and-stride-the-bookkeeping-with-a-payoff}

@sec-07-filters-convolution left a practical problem: a $k \times k$ kernel on an $n \times n$ image
yields only $(n-k+1) \times (n-k+1)$ outputs, because the window must stay inside the
frame. For one layer this is a small loss. For a deep stack it is fatal: unpadded
$5 \times 5$ convolutions take a $28 \times 28$ image to 24, 20, 16, 12, 8 and then 4 pixels
on a side, and a seventh layer would leave nothing.

Unpadded convolution also treats pixels unequally. A pixel enters one dot product for every
window position that covers it, and near the border there are fewer such positions: a corner
pixel is covered by a single window, an interior pixel by $k^2$. Border pixels therefore
contribute fewer terms to the output, and receive fewer gradient terms, than central ones.

The remedy is **padding**: a border of extra pixels, usually zeros, added around the input
before the window slides. Padding serves two purposes. It decouples depth from shrinkage, so a
network can be deep without its feature maps vanishing. It also narrows the border imbalance:
for a $3 \times 3$ kernel with one pixel of padding, a corner pixel enters 4 windows and an
edge pixel 6, against 9 in the interior. For our $5 \times 5$ kernels, a 2-pixel border keeps
a $28 \times 28$ image at $28 \times 28$, which is why the first convolutional layer above
uses `padding=2`.

Sometimes we want to shrink a map on purpose: coarser maps cost less computation, and every
later window then covers more of the image. **Stride** moves the window $s$ pixels at a time
instead of one. A stride of 2 roughly halves each spatial dimension and divides the number of
activations by about four. A strided convolution downsamples with learned weights; pooling
downsamples with a fixed rule. Padding, kernel size and stride enter one formula:

$$
n_{\text{out}} \;=\; \left\lfloor \frac{n + 2p - k}{s} \right\rfloor + 1 .
$$ {#eq-outsize}

Padding restores the output positions that the window would otherwise lose; stride
skips stops on purpose.
The numerator is the padded length minus the window, i.e. how far the window can
travel; dividing by the step and flooring counts the stops; $+1$ counts the starting
position. Three worked cases make the arithmetic visible:

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Create a random 8×8 single-channel image `x8` as a batch of one.
2. Implement the output-size formula, three regimes.
:::

```{python}
#| label: shapes
#| code-summary: "Code: the output-size formula, three regimes"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
x8 = torch.randn(1, 1, 8, 8)
# [2]
for p, s in [(0, 1), (1, 1), (1, 2)]:
    out = F.conv2d(x8, torch.randn(1, 1, 3, 3), padding=p, stride=s)
    n_out = (8 + 2 * p - 3) // s + 1
    print(f"n=8, k=3, p={p}, s={s}:  formula {n_out}  torch {tuple(out.shape[2:])}")
```
::::
## Pooling: trading exact location for local tolerance

@sec-07-filters-convolution established that stride-one
convolution is translation-equivariant on the interior under
matched boundary rules: shifting the input shifts the feature map.
For classification, we also want the final decision to remain
stable under the small, label-preserving shifts considered in @sec-06-generalization-inductive-bias.

**Pooling** summarizes a neighborhood of each feature map
with one number. It reduces spatial resolution and can make some
local rearrangements irrelevant to the pooled output. Whether
that produces useful shift tolerance depends on the activations,
window alignment, and subsequent layers. Two summaries are common,
and neither has parameters:

- **Max pooling** keeps the largest activation in each window and discards
  the rest.
- **Average pooling** takes the mean of each window. The result is smoother,
  but a single large activation is diluted by small neighbors.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Fill a 4×4 grid `t` with the values 0 through 15, row by row.
2. Max and average pooling on a known grid.
:::

```{python}
#| label: pooling
#| code-summary: "Code: max and average pooling on a known grid"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
t = torch.arange(16.).reshape(1, 1, 4, 4)
# [2]
print(f"input:\n{t.squeeze()}")
print(f"max pool 2x2:\n{F.max_pool2d(t, 2).squeeze()}")
print(f"avg pool 2x2:\n{F.avg_pool2d(t, 2).squeeze()}")
```
::::
The common configuration is the one above: $2 \times 2$ windows with stride 2,
non-overlapping, halving each spatial dimension. Our LeNet uses max pooling. Exercise 4 compares it with average
pooling under the same training recipe.

How can this give local tolerance? Start with a deliberately clean construction in
which max pooling removes the effect of a shift:

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Place clues of 9 and 3 on a blank 4×4 `scene`, and build `shifted` with both moved
   one pixel right.
2. Run one constructed shift that pooling cannot see.
:::

```{python}
#| label: pool-invariance
#| code-summary: "Code: one constructed shift that pooling cannot see"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
scene = torch.zeros(1, 1, 4, 4)
scene[0, 0, 1, 0] = 9.0        # a strong clue, upper-left region
scene[0, 0, 2, 2] = 3.0        # a weaker clue, lower-right region

shifted = torch.zeros_like(scene)
shifted[0, 0, 1, 1] = 9.0      # both clues moved one pixel right
shifted[0, 0, 2, 3] = 3.0

# [2]
print(f"pooled original: {F.max_pool2d(scene,   2).squeeze().tolist()}")
print(f"pooled shifted:  {F.max_pool2d(shifted, 2).squeeze().tolist()}")
```
::::
Both activations moved, yet these particular pooled maps are *identical*: each isolated
maximum stayed inside its $2 \times 2$ window. That equality belongs to this
construction, not to max pooling in general. A shift can change which values share a
window, which maximum wins, or what crosses the boundary. Pooling can therefore absorb
some jitter, but the amount depends on the activations and alignment;
we test the complete network on shifted garments rather than assume
tolerance.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pooling reduces spatial detail

Pooling retains a coarse spatial grid while discarding information
within each window. This can be useful when exact position is
irrelevant to the task, but it can also remove distinctions needed
for recognition or localization. The choice of pooling operation
and resolution therefore belongs in the experimental comparison.
:::

## Receptive fields grow with depth {#how-far-a-deep-neuron-sees}

Stacking has one more consequence: it resolves the tension @sec-06-generalization-inductive-bias
left us with. Every kernel here is tiny and local: $5 \times 5$. Yet
recognizing a garment is a *global* judgment. Where does globality come from?

From depth. A neuron in the first feature map depends on a $5 \times 5$ patch of the image:
its **receptive field**. A neuron one layer up depends on a $5 \times 5$ patch *of feature
maps*, each pixel of which already summarizes a patch below $\rightarrow$ its
receptive field on the original image is wider. Pooling accelerates this: after a
$2\times2$/stride-2 pool, neighboring pixels in the pooled map stand two original
pixels apart, so every later window covers twice the ground. For our upcoming network
the count runs: conv1 covers $5 \times 5$ $\rightarrow$ pooling nudges it to $6 \times
6$ $\rightarrow$ conv2's $5\times5$ window, at stride-2 spacing, expands it to $14
\times 14$ $\rightarrow$ the final pool reaches $16 \times 16$, over half the frame
in every direction, using only $5 \times 5$ kernels.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-receptive-field
#| fig-alt: "Four nested outline boxes are drawn concentric on a coat image. Their side lengths grow from five pixels after the first convolution to six after the first pool, fourteen after the second convolution, and sixteen after the final pool. Convolution stages are drawn solid and pooling stages dotted."
#| fig-cap: "Receptive fields by depth. Each box is the patch of the input that one unit depends on after a stage, drawn concentric for comparison. On the coat, the nested fields cross visible sleeves, torso, and boundary. One unit depends on a 5×5 patch after conv1, 6×6 after the first pool, 14×14 after conv2, and 16×16 after the final pool. Local wiring yields increasingly large fields; the dense head then combines all 25 overlapping final fields at once."
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 3.6), dpi=450)
example_index = 3                              # a coat, not the earlier sandal
ax.imshow(X_val[example_index, 0], cmap="gray")
# One unit's receptive field after each stage; boxes are drawn concentric, so the
# even sizes sit half a pixel off the pixel grid.
for size, color, style, lab in [(5, "#232D4B", "-", "after conv1: 5×5"),
                                (6, "#232D4B", ":", "after pool1: 6×6"),
                                (14, "#5379AA", "-", "after conv2: 14×14"),
                                (16, "#5379AA", ":", "after pool2: 16×16")]:
    lo = 14 - size / 2
    ax.add_patch(mpatches.Rectangle((lo, lo), size, size, fill=False,
                                    lw=2.4 if style == ":" else 2, linestyle=style,
                                    edgecolor=color, label=lab))
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5),
          title="receptive field", title_fontsize=8)
ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
This is the compositional hierarchy of @sec-03-nonlinearity-mlp, now encouraged by
the architecture. MLP layers also compose features. Convolution adds local
connectivity and spatial sharing to that composition, and growing receptive fields let
later layers compose earlier responses over larger regions. Learned channels often progress from edge-like patterns to
textures and parts, but the architecture does not force those human labels. The CNN
combines information across the frame gradually, through depth.^[Attention (@sec-13-attention)
combines information across the whole input in a single step, at a different cost.]

## LeNet: the whole machine

The canonical blueprint is **LeNet**, Yann LeCun's digit-reading
network, and its rhythm is the CNN design pattern to this day: *convolve, shrink,
deepen; repeat; then decide.* Spatial size falls (28 $\rightarrow$ 14 $\rightarrow$ 5)
while feature depth grows (1 $\rightarrow$ 6 $\rightarrow$ 16): the network trades
"where" for "what" stage by stage, until a small dense head maps the final $16 \times
5 \times 5$ summary to class scores.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. LeNet.
:::

```{python}
#| label: lenet
#| code-summary: "Code: LeNet"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
class LeNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 6, 5, padding=2)  # (N,1,28,28)->(N,6,28,28)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(6, 16, 5)            # (N,6,14,14)->(N,16,10,10)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(16 * 5 * 5, 120)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(120, 84)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(84, 10)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv1(x)), 2)   # -> (N, 6, 14, 14)
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv2(x)), 2)   # -> (N, 16, 5, 5)
        x = x.flatten(1)                             # -> (N, 400)
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
        return self.fc3(x)                           # logits, (N, 10)
```
::::
Every line is a tool we already own: @eq-conv-layer twice, @eq-outsize behind
the choice of `padding=2`, pooling twice, then @sec-03-nonlinearity-mlp's MLP as the
decision head. The
convolutional layers form the backbone, and `fc1` through `fc3` replace @sec-02-logistic-softmax's
single linear head with a small MLP. Per @sec-02-logistic-softmax's advice, the model returns raw
logits and lets `F.cross_entropy` handle the probabilities.

::: {.callout-note}
## LeNet, then and now

The LeNet family (LeCun and colleagues, 1989–1998) began by reading handwritten ZIP
codes for the US Postal Service, and its mature form, LeNet-5, went on to read a
substantial share of America's bank checks. Our variant keeps the classic
skeleton but changes its internals: ReLU where the original used sigmoid-family activations
(@sec-03-nonlinearity-mlp, @sec-05-backpropagation), max pooling where it used
subsampling based on averaging, Adam as the optimizer. Our later CNNs add one more
modern stabilizer, batch normalization, which we meet properly in @sec-09-modern-cnns-transfer.
:::

Before training, we count the parameters: weight sharing in @sec-07-filters-convolution
should save many, and @sec-06-generalization-inductive-bias's MLP is the yardstick:

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Define the reusable `make_mlp` helper.
2. Instantiate a fresh `LeNet` and a fresh MLP from `make_mlp`.
3. Parameter audit, LeNet vs. @sec-06-generalization-inductive-bias's MLP.
:::

```{python}
#| label: params
#| code-summary: "Code: parameter audit, LeNet vs. Chapter 6's MLP"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
def make_mlp() -> nn.Sequential:
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(),
                         nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10))

# [2]
lenet, mlp = LeNet(), make_mlp()
# [3]
for name, p in lenet.named_parameters():
    print(f"{name:14s} {str(tuple(p.shape)):16s} {p.numel():>7,}")
n_conv = sum(p.numel() for n, p in lenet.named_parameters() if "conv" in n)
n_lenet = sum(p.numel() for p in lenet.parameters())
n_mlp = sum(p.numel() for p in mlp.parameters())
print(f"\nLeNet: {n_lenet:,} parameters ({n_conv:,} of them convolutional)")
print(f"MLP:   {n_mlp:,} parameters")
```
::::
These parameter counts can be read two ways. Against the MLP of @sec-06-generalization-inductive-bias,
rebuilt here as `make_mlp` (the network of that chapter with an `nn.Flatten()` in front: 784
inputs, 256 hidden ReLU units and 10 outputs), LeNet carries 61,706 parameters to the MLP's
203,530 (less than a third) while performing far richer spatial computation. This is the saving
that @sec-07-filters-convolution's matrix view showed. Within LeNet, the two convolutional
layers, which compute the spatial features, hold 2,572 parameters (about 4%), and the dense
head holds the rest. We reduce that imbalance in @sec-09-modern-cnns-transfer, where modern
architectures go deeper in convolution and lighter in the head.

Now train both models under one shared optimization recipe: same fitting split,
optimizer, minibatch size, number of epochs, and therefore number of parameter updates.
The comparison does **not** match parameter count or floating-point work; a convolution
and a dense layer spend different computation per update. Architecture is the intended
difference; compute is not controlled:

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Define the reusable helpers: `train_model` and `accuracy`.
2. Run one recipe, two architectures.
3. Print train and validation accuracy for the MLP and for LeNet.
:::

```{python}
#| label: train-both
#| code-summary: "Code: one recipe, two architectures"
#| code-fold: false
from dlbook.supervised import fit_supervised   # Listing 4.1

# [1]
def train_model(
    model_fn, X_fit: torch.Tensor = X_tr, y_fit: torch.Tensor = y_tr,
    epochs: int = 150, batch: int = 128, seed: int = 6050
) -> nn.Module:
    # Listing 4.1 verbatim; this chapter's deltas are the budget (150
    # epochs, batch 128) and, below, the models that get trained.
    return fit_supervised(
        model_fn, X_fit, y_fit, epochs=epochs, batch=batch, seed=seed
    )

@torch.no_grad()
def accuracy(model: nn.Module, X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor) -> float:
    model.eval()
    return (model(X).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()

# [2]
mlp = train_model(make_mlp)
lenet = train_model(LeNet)
# [3]
for name, model in [("MLP  ", mlp), ("LeNet", lenet)]:
    print(f"{name}  train {accuracy(model, X_tr, y_tr):.1%}   "
          f"validation {accuracy(model, X_val, y_val):.1%}")
```
::::
Read the clean-validation column: the MLP scores 75.5% and LeNet 74.5% in this
single seeded run. A one-point difference is descriptive, not an uncertainty estimate,
so it does not establish which architecture has higher expected clean accuracy.
Both models nearly interpolate the fitting split. Our small-data
regime makes a narrower point: LeNet reaches comparable clean accuracy with less than a
third of the parameters. The shift experiment now compares the two models on shifted
garments.

## LeNet under the two-pixel shift {#the-rematch}

In @sec-06-generalization-inductive-bias, shifting every validation image two pixels to the
right took our MLP from 76.0% to 46.5% accuracy. We now give LeNet the same test. Retrained
here on LeNet's schedule, the MLP starts from 75.5% clean validation accuracy and LeNet from
74.5%, so the two begin level. The question is whether the convolutional structure makes the
classifier more tolerant of the shift.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Define the reusable `shift_right` helper.
2. Compute `acc_mlp` and `acc_cnn`, validation accuracy under right shifts of 0 to 4
   pixels.
3. Plot accuracy vs. shift, both models.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-cliff-rematch
#| fig-alt: "Two accuracy curves decline as images shift right. They begin at similar clean accuracy, but the LeNet curve stays above the MLP curve at every nonzero shift; a dotted horizontal line marks chance."
#| fig-cap: "Validation accuracy under right shifts. Both architectures use the same optimizer schedule, though not matched compute. At two pixels the MLP falls from 75.5% to 42.0%, while LeNet falls from 74.5% to 57.5%. The dotted line is chance."
#| code-summary: "Code: accuracy vs. shift, both models"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
def shift_right(X: torch.Tensor, px: int) -> torch.Tensor:
    out = torch.zeros_like(X)
    if px == 0:
        return X.clone()
    out[..., px:] = X[..., :-px]
    return out

# [2]
shifts = list(range(5))
acc_mlp = [accuracy(mlp, shift_right(X_val, s), y_val) for s in shifts]
acc_cnn = [accuracy(lenet, shift_right(X_val, s), y_val) for s in shifts]
# [3]
for s in shifts:
    print(f"shift {s}px:   MLP {acc_mlp[s]:.1%}   LeNet {acc_cnn[s]:.1%}")

plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 3.2))
plt.plot(shifts, acc_mlp, "o-", color="#E57200", lw=2, ms=7, label="MLP (Ch. 6)")
plt.plot(shifts, acc_cnn, "s-", color="#232D4B", lw=2, ms=7, label="LeNet")
plt.axhline(0.1, ls=":", color="#B8B8A8")
plt.xlabel("shift (pixels right)"); plt.ylabel("validation accuracy")
plt.ylim(0, 0.9); plt.xticks(shifts); plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
::::
LeNet stays above the MLP at every nonzero shift, and the gap is largest at two and three
pixels. At one pixel the two are close, 66.0% for LeNet and 64.0% for the MLP. At two pixels
the MLP loses 33.5 points and LeNet 17.0; at three, LeNet scores 42.0% against 27.0%, and at
four, 23.0% against 18.5%. These numbers come from one deterministic validation split, not a
sampling distribution, but the within-run contrast is large.

The comparison changes the complete architecture, so it does not isolate the contributions of
locality, weight sharing, pooling or the classifier head. Several operations can still
introduce shift sensitivity: cropping and padding affect the responses at the border, pooling
depends on window alignment, and the dense head gives each spatial position retained after
flattening its own weights. @sec-09-modern-cnns-transfer replaces that position-sensitive
head with global pooling.

In @sec-06-generalization-inductive-bias, the MLP's first-layer weights were full-frame
templates with broad, diffuse patterns. @fig-learned-filters shows the six $5 \times 5$
kernels of LeNet's first layer and, under each, its feature map after the ReLU on the coat
of @fig-receptive-field, a validation image.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Extract first-layer kernels and their feature maps.
:::

```{python}
#| label: learned-filter-values
#| code-summary: "Code: first-layer kernels and their feature maps"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
example_index = 3                                   # the Figure 9.3 coat
img = X_val[example_index:example_index + 1]
with torch.no_grad():
    fmaps = F.relu(lenet.conv1(img)).squeeze(0)     # (6, 28, 28)
kernels = lenet.conv1.weight.detach().squeeze(1)    # (6, 5, 5)
```
::::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-learned-filters
#| fig-alt: "Six small signed kernel heatmaps form the top row, and six larger activation maps for the same coat form the bottom row. The response maps emphasize different local regions even where the kernels remain diffuse."
#| fig-cap: "What LeNet's first layer learned. Top: six first-layer 5×5 kernels (red positive, blue negative). Bottom: their feature maps on the coat of @fig-receptive-field, a validation image whose sleeves and torso make spatial responses easy to compare. The maps respond differently, but several kernels remain diffuse and should not be over-interpreted."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(9, 3.2))
lim = kernels.abs().max()
for i in range(6):
    axes[0, i].imshow(kernels[i], cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-lim, vmax=lim)
    axes[1, i].imshow(fmaps[i], cmap="gray")
    axes[0, i].axis("off"); axes[1, i].axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
The six local kernels produce distinct response maps on the same image. Some show directional
structure; others remain noisy enough that naming them as detectors would claim more than this
one run supports. Nobody designed them: they result from optimizer steps on the
classification loss, with gradients flowing backward through @eq-conv-layer.

## One sealed test check

With both architectures, the optimizer schedule, the shift size and the two reported metrics
fixed, we refit each model on all 1,200 development images with the same training budget, open
the 600-image test set once, and score each refit model on the clean test images and on the
same images shifted two pixels right. *Sealed* is chapter-local here: these 600 images also
serve other chapters as an endpoint, as [the experiment
interlude](../interludes/learning-by-experiment.qmd) explains, but no choice in this chapter
looked at them.

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Run one final test-set check.
2. Print clean and two-pixel-shifted test accuracy for the refit MLP and LeNet.
:::

```{python}
#| label: final-holdout
#| code-summary: "Code: one final test-set check"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
mlp_final = train_model(make_mlp, X_dev, y_dev)
lenet_final = train_model(LeNet, X_dev, y_dev)
# [2]
for name, model in [("MLP  ", mlp_final), ("LeNet", lenet_final)]:
    print(f"{name}  clean {accuracy(model, X_test, y_test):.1%}   "
          f"shift-2 {accuracy(model, shift_right(X_test, 2), y_test):.1%}")
```
::::
The sealed check confirms the validation comparison. On clean test images the MLP scores
82.2% and LeNet 82.5%, a descriptive 0.3-point gap from one seed. Under the predeclared
two-pixel shift the MLP falls to 41.8% and LeNet to 62.3%, with less than a third of the
MLP's parameters.

::: {.callout-note}
## Check yourself

Close the book for one minute and rebuild the CNN.

- Which kernel entries become learnable, and which convolutional structure remains built in?
- What do channels, pooling, and receptive-field growth each contribute?
- What does the shift comparison establish under this recipe, and why does it not isolate one architectural constraint?
:::

## Okay, so: the kernel became learnable

1. **One change**: the kernel's numbers became parameters.
   Gradient descent can recover a hand-crafted detector from data (our rigged game)
   and, more importantly, learn kernels nobody designed, supervised only by the
   task loss at the far end.
2. **Channels turn one detector into many**: out-channels stack the feature maps
   of several kernels; in-channels let each next-layer kernel combine all maps at once
   (@eq-conv-layer).
3. **Padding and stride are the shape budget**: $n_{\text{out}} = \lfloor (n + 2p -
   k)/s \rfloor + 1$ (@eq-outsize). Padding lets networks go deep without shrinking to
   nothing; stride shrinks on purpose.
4. **Pooling summarizes each window by one number**: max pooling keeps the largest
   activation and discards its exact position within the window. Any resulting shift
   tolerance depends on the activations, window alignment, and later layers.
5. **Receptive fields grow with depth**: $5 \rightarrow 6 \rightarrow 14 \rightarrow
   16$ in our LeNet. Stacked local layers cover more of the frame at each stage. Like the MLP layers of @sec-03-nonlinearity-mlp,
   they compose features, now with local connectivity and
   spatial sharing.
6. **The verdict**: on the sealed test set, one seed puts clean accuracy at 82.2% for
   the MLP and 82.5% for LeNet; this does not establish an expected clean-accuracy
   difference. Under the predeclared two-pixel shift, the same models score 41.8% and
   62.3%. Under this training recipe, LeNet achieves higher accuracy on
   the shifted images with fewer parameters. This compares the
   two complete models, rather than isolating one architectural
   constraint.

Most of LeNet's parameters remain in its dense head, and its
accuracy still declines under image shifts. The next chapter
examines smaller classifier heads, deeper convolutional networks,
and the training choices needed to compare them.

## Sources and further reading {.unnumbered}

- LeCun et al.,
  ["Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition"](https://doi.org/10.1109/5.726791)
  (1998): the primary LeNet account, including the architecture's document-recognition
  setting.
- Fukushima,
  ["Neocognitron: A Self-organizing Neural Network Model"](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00344251)
  (1980): historical context for alternating feature extraction and spatial tolerance.
- Zeiler and Fergus,
  ["Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.2901)
  (2014): methods and evidence for inspecting learned convolutional features without
  over-reading a single filter image.
- Dumoulin and Visin,
  ["A Guide to Convolution Arithmetic for Deep Learning"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.07285)
  (2016): a compact companion for checking convolution, pooling, and receptive-field
  shapes.
